extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers and novelists interested in writing epistolary novels
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and drafting novels told through documents (letters, diaries, texts, reports, transcripts, etc.), including choices about form, point(s) of view, document types, pacing, and voice. Focused on craft decisions that make epistolary storytelling effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on your epistolary style
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s hard to figure out what story you should tell and the method you want to use to tell it at the same time... You want to think about the shape or form your story will take.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide up front whether you'll use only one document type (e.g., journal entries) or a mix (diaries, newspaper articles, doctor notes, correspondence, transcripts, etc.). Consider whether to pants it or plan — pantsing is possible but will require much more revising. Think about how the chosen form shapes the story and what kinds of documents best communicate your characters and world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose document types that reflect characters and world
rubrics_metrics.description: “What kinds of writing would these characters interact with daily? Does your hero write a letter to their love interest, or is an instant message more appropriate?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select documents consistent with the time period, profession, and daily life of characters (texts, emails, papyrus, clinical files, police reports, social media). You may incorporate images (e.g., papyrus) and should pick formats that feel authentic for the setting and help convey information naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide on POV and number of voices (monologic/dialogic/polylogic)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Epistolary novels can be told from one character’s Point of View (POV), or told from two or more POVs... think about whether you want your story to be monologic, dialogic, or polylogic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose single or multiple narrators depending on whether you need one voice or multiple perspectives. A dialogic/polylogic approach allows contrasting accounts and can support multiple timelines or conflicting memories; monologic keeps a single intimate voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to be fully epistolary or mix with conventional narration
rubrics_metrics.description: “Novels can be written entirely in epistolary form using just letters or a mix of different document types, or they can be written as a narrative interspersed with other documents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh pros/cons of fully epistolary (consistent voice, constraints) versus a hybrid (e.g., The Martian mixes logs with third-person chapters). Mixing lets you step outside documents when needed and can clarify events other characters don't directly record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhance the narration with purposeful mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: “One way to play around and experiment with epistolary novels is by including intentional mistakes in the documents.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic errors (wrong recipient texts/emails, typos, autocorrect changes, grammar slips) deliberately to create conflict, humor, or reveal character traits. Even minor errors can change meaning (example: “bird” vs “bride”)—use that to drive plot surprises or character embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make documents your own (use templates but edit for story)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Depending on the type of documents you want to include in your novel, you can find some templates online... Don’t be afraid to omit parts of documents or templates and make them your own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use real-world templates (police reports, legal files) for authenticity but cut or alter sections (disclaimers, excessive formality) that would slow pacing or provide irrelevant detail. Fiction permits liberties—readers will suspend disbelief if the document serves the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal internal and external conflict through documents
rubrics_metrics.description: “A diary or journal entry can be a great natural way to reveal that secret to the reader... You can reveal external conflict through epistolary writing as well.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use private documents to disclose secrets or inner thoughts characters won't say aloud. Use other documents (letters, government notices) to show external pressures—e.g., censorship causing letters to shorten (Ella Minnow Pea). Documents can expose both psychological state and social forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid repeating information; ensure each document contributes new material
rubrics_metrics.description: “One thing to keep in mind when you’re using this format is you don’t want to repeat the same information twice... these documents should help enhance your story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure documents advance plot, character, or theme. If a document only restates known facts, it becomes redundant and slows pacing. Use each entry to reveal something new or to deepen understanding, not to recap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use documents and multiple timelines to build atmosphere and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is also great to use when writing a story that has multiple timelines in it... The Dead House tells the story through diaries, newspaper clippings, doctor notes... and breaks up the novel into two alternating timelines.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interleave different document types and timelines to create tension, contrast, and mood. Alternate pre- and post-event documents to withhold/ reveal information and manipulate reader perspective and suspense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study famous epistolary stories and map their structural beats
rubrics_metrics.description: “Read and study books in different formats... Try to identify the structure or beats in these novels as well. How are the foundational beats represented?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze successful examples (Dracula, The Martian, Daisy Jones & The Six, The Dead House) to see how they represent inciting incidents, turning points, and resolutions through documents. Note which beats use which document types and how documents substitute for typical scene/beat functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the form to convey narrator reliability and character psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Implied throughout: using diaries/transcripts can create a unique insight into a character’s fragile and vulnerable mental state or produce an unreliable narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage first-person documents to show memory lapses, omissions, edits, or contradictions that suggest unreliability. Documentary forms (transcripts, reports) can contrast with personal writings to highlight discrepancies and deepen mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance realism with readability (cut legalese and irrelevant detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those files may include pages and pages of disclaimer information that you just don’t need... This will help you avoid slowing down your pace with useless information.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize story clarity and momentum over verbatim realism. Trim or fictionalize bureaucratic material; only include details that serve atmosphere, character, or plot. Readers will accept abbreviated or altered documents if they serve narrative purpose.
